opus-5.5.text:
I think long context is one of the most fundamental problems right now, more important than many people realize. If you think about what we want these models to do, which is to act more like an agent, carry out long-horizon tasks, and read a whole codebase or a whole set of documents, then context length is basically the model's working memory. If the memory is short, there's a ceiling on how complex a task it can do, no matter how smart it is within each step.

Architecturally, the core tension comes from attention. Full attention is very expressive, because every token can look at every other token, but its cost grows quadratically with sequence length, and at inference time the KV cache grows linearly and becomes a memory bottleneck. So you have a tradeoff between expressiveness and efficiency, and most architectural work in this area is about where to sit on that curve.

There are a few broad directions. One is to keep full attention and make it cheaper through engineering: better kernels, better parallelism across devices, compressing or quantizing the KV cache. That gets you surprisingly far. Another is sparse attention, where each token only attends to a selected subset of the context, ideally chosen dynamically by the model rather than by a fixed pattern. A third is linear attention or state-space-style models, which compress history into a fixed-size state. They're very efficient, but historically they've been weaker at precise retrieval, finding one exact detail far back in the context. That's why hybrid architectures are attractive: mostly efficient layers, with a few full-attention layers to keep retrieval ability.

But I'd emphasize that architecture is only half the problem. Even if your model can technically accept a million tokens, the question is whether it actually uses them well. That depends a lot on data and training. You need training signal where the long-range information really matters. Otherwise the model learns to rely only on the local context, and the long context is decoration. Evaluation is tricky too. Needle-in-a-haystack tests are a start, but real tasks need reasoning across many pieces of information spread through the context, not just retrieving one fact.

And now with reinforcement learning and long chains of thought, long context matters even more, because the model generates very long outputs and has to keep its own reasoning coherent. So the context is no longer just input you read once; it's something the model is constantly writing to and reading from. That changes the efficiency requirements, especially for decoding.

So my view is that long context is not a single trick. It's a co-design problem across architecture, systems, data, and training objectives. And I believe whoever solves it well, making very long context both cheap and actually useful, will have a big advantage in the next stage, where models do long, autonomous work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tradeoffs between attention expressiveness and efficiency, but does not say that improving long-context performance may degrade short-context performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think long context is really one of the most fundamental problems in this field, and I'd break it into a few layers.

The first layer is the obvious one: the attention mechanism scales quadratically with sequence length. When I was working on Transformer-XL and later XLNet, this was already the central tension. Transformer-XL's segment-level recurrence and relative positional encoding were one early attempt to let the model see further back without paying the full cost every time. But recurrence and caching only get you so far. You're essentially trading off between a fixed-size memory that compresses the past and a full memory that grows with the input.

The second layer, which I think is underappreciated, is that long context is not just about whether the model can technically attend to a token ten thousand or a million positions away. It's about whether the model can actually use that information. Many architectures claim a long window, but if you test them with a needle-in-a-haystack task or a multi-hop reasoning task across the whole document, performance collapses. So the real challenge is "lossless" long context, meaning the model's ability to retrieve, reason, and compose information should not degrade as the context grows. That requires attention to the training data, the positional encoding scheme, and the way you scale from short-context pretraining to long-context fine-tuning. Just extrapolating position embeddings often produces a model that technically runs but doesn't really understand.

The third layer is systems. At a million tokens, the KV cache alone becomes a memory bottleneck for inference, and the prefill cost is enormous. So you need architectural choices that are friendly to real serving: sparse or hybrid attention patterns, grouped or multi-query attention to shrink the cache, better kernels, and sometimes rethinking whether every layer needs full attention at all. Architecture and infrastructure can no longer be designed separately.

What I find exciting is that long context changes what a model fundamentally is. A model with a short window is like someone with no working memory beyond a few sentences. Once you have reliable long context, the model can read an entire codebase, an entire book, a full conversation history, and the boundary between "knowledge inside the parameters" and "information in the context" starts to blur. I think of long context as a kind of new dimension of scaling, alongside parameters and data. Moving from short context to effectively unlimited context is as significant a step as the move from small to large models.

So, to summarize, the challenge is threefold: the computational cost, the question of real understanding rather than nominal window length, and the systems problem of serving it. All three have to be solved together, and I think the field is only partway there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long-context costs and scaling from short-context pretraining, but does not say that improving long-context performance may degrade short-context performance.

astra-6.text:
I think the main challenge is that supporting long context is more than increasing the context window. You need to make it computationally affordable, and you need the model to actually use the information in that window.

With standard attention, computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache also grows as the context gets longer, which puts pressure on memory and bandwidth. So there are architectural trade-offs: you can use sparse attention, compress older information, or introduce some form of recurrent memory. But whenever you reduce the cost by discarding or compressing information, you have to ask whether the model can still recover a detail that becomes important later.

And architecture is only part of it. The training data and training objectives need to teach the model to connect information across long distances. Finding one relevant sentence in a long document is useful, but combining evidence from many different parts is a harder problem.

So I would look at efficiency and capability together. The goal is not simply to fit more tokens into the model. It is to make those additional tokens useful at a reasonable cost.

r001.rationale: The response discusses efficiency and information-retention trade-offs for long contexts, but does not say that improving long-context performance may degrade short-context performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key challenge is that a longer context window has to be both computationally affordable and useful. In a standard Transformer, attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so simply increasing the window becomes expensive very quickly. During generation, the KV cache also grows with the context, which puts pressure on memory and memory bandwidth.

But efficiency is only one part of the problem. Even if you can fit a very long sequence into the model, that doesn’t mean the model can reliably use all of it. It needs to find relevant information, connect details across distant passages, and avoid getting distracted by irrelevant content. That makes long context a training and evaluation problem as well as an architectural one.

So I would think about these things together: efficient attention, memory management, and training tasks that actually require long-range reasoning. The goal is to make additional context improve the answer, rather than just increase the number of tokens the model accepts.

r001.rationale: The response discusses efficiency, memory, and reliable use of long contexts, but does not say that improving long-context performance may degrade short-context performance.
